analysis.one_liner: Cut corporate and estate taxes, froze new federal regulations until unemployment fell, and opened more federal land and water to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 59 Republican cosponsors in the House, was referred to eight committees and never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Jobs Through Growth Act was a broad package of tax and regulatory changes introduced by Rep. Scott Garrett in November 2011 as a Republican response to the President's jobs proposals. It would have cut the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 25%, repealed the estate tax permanently, let individuals opt into a simplified income tax with a 15% and 25% bracket, and let companies bring overseas profits home at reduced tax. It also would have blocked federal agencies from issuing significant new regulations until unemployment dropped to 7.7% or below, let small businesses opt out of new federal rules, and required Congress to approve every major new regulation before it could take effect. On the energy side, it would have opened more of the Gulf of Mexico and the Arctic to oil and gas drilling, allowed oil shale leasing on federal land, removed the EPA's authority to regulate greenhouse gases, and forced expedited approval of the Keystone XL pipeline.
analysis.who_benefits: Large corporations would get a lower 35% to 25% top tax rate and a temporary deduction on profits brought back from overseas subsidiaries (conditioned on maintaining U.S. employment levels). Wealthy families would benefit from permanent repeal of the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes. High-income individuals would benefit from the optional flat 15%/25% tax system, repeal of the individual alternative minimum tax, and inflation indexing of capital gains. Oil, gas, and coal companies would gain access to new federal leases offshore, in the Arctic, and on federal oil shale lands, plus faster permitting and the Keystone XL pipeline approval. Small businesses would gain expanded exemptions from new federal rules and new tools to sue and delay agency regulations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporations, wealthy estates, and energy companies

how_it_helps.text: Cut the top corporate tax rate from 35% to 25%.
Repealed the estate and generation-skipping transfer taxes and made a $5 million gift-tax exemption permanent, eliminating the tax on large inherited estates.

Let individuals elect a simplified alternative income tax with 15% and 25% brackets, repealed the alternative minimum tax for individuals, and allowed inflation indexing of capital gains on assets held more than three years.

Froze significant federal regulatory actions until the unemployment rate fell to 7.7% or below, required Congress to affirmatively approve every major new federal rule before it could take effect, exempted small businesses from new rules, and expanded small businesses' ability to sue agencies.

Opened more of the Gulf of Mexico, the Arctic Coastal Plain, and federal lands to oil and gas leasing, ordered oil shale lease sales, barred EPA regulation of greenhouse gases, and directed expedited approval of the Keystone XL pipeline.

analysis.who_pays: Federal revenue would fall substantially from the corporate rate cut, estate tax repeal, and individual tax changes, increasing deficits or requiring spending cuts elsewhere. Workers and the public would lose the protections of rules that could no longer be issued—covering areas like air quality, worker safety, and consumer protection—until unemployment fell below 7.7%. Environmental and public-health protections would be directly weakened, since the bill removes the EPA's authority to regulate greenhouse gases and blocks new significant rules.

drawbacks.text: The regulatory moratorium would have blocked any significant federal rule—including rules on public health, safety, and the environment—until quarterly unemployment fell to 7.7%, regardless of the merit of the rule.
Businesses with 200 or fewer employees could have elected exemption from federal regulations issued after 2008, and the bill let small businesses sue to stop rules before they were finalized.
The simplified individual income tax capped the top rate at 25% and made the 15% capital gains rate permanent—rates that primarily reduce taxes on high-income households and investors.

The bill did not include a mechanism to pay for the tax cuts beyond instructing the Ways and Means Committee to someday report legislation broadening the corporate tax base, leaving the revenue loss open-ended.

The REINS-style subtitle would have required both chambers of Congress and the President to affirmatively approve every major new rule within 70 days or it would die, a structure that in practice stops nearly all major regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated purpose was job creation, but its actual provisions mostly reduced taxes on corporations, capital gains, and inherited wealth and rolled back rules covering pollution, workplace, and consumer protections, with no offsetting revenue provisions in the bill itself. The strongest good-faith argument for parts of it—corporate rate reduction and the optional 15/25 simplified tax—has real merit and was later adopted in broad form by bipartisan tax reform. But the regulatory freeze tied to a 7.7% unemployment threshold and the small-business exemption from federal law went well beyond targeting red tape, and the estate tax repeal would concentrate wealth further. On balance, the costs to public protections and revenue outweighed the growth benefits, which is not to say every provision was without merit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to eight House committees on the day it was introduced, and no committee ever reported it out, so it never came to a vote before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 10, 2011 and referred to the Ways and Means Committee plus seven other committees.
It was subsequently referred to several subcommittees, including the Subcommittee on Energy and Power and the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources.
The last action in the record is the November 29, 2011 subcommittee referral; no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred.
The bill attracted 59 Republican cosponsors in the House, all from the same party.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses and industries that would have benefited from lower taxes and lighter federal regulation are no better off; the outcome preserved the status quo of existing environmental, financial, and workplace rules that the bill would have rolled back.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing federal regulatory protections stayed intact

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Jobs Through Growth Act in the House on November 10, 2011.

for.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or brought the bill to a vote after it was referred to eight committees on the day it was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: All 60 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill never advanced in a chamber controlled by a Democratic Senate majority at the time.

industries.note: The bill opened the Gulf, Arctic Coastal Plain, and federal lands to new leasing, extended dormant leases, sped up permitting, and expedited the Keystone XL pipeline. These provisions expand access to publicly owned resources for private drilling.

A 25% corporate rate, a temporary deduction on foreign dividends, and capital gains inflation indexing directly cut taxes on corporate profits and investment income. The employment-maintenance condition on the foreign-dividend deduction was the oneStrings-attached element.
Estate and generation-skipping tax repeal plus a permanent 35% gift tax rate and $5 million exemption would eliminate most tax on inherited wealth.

The bill granted small businesses expanded rights to challenge and be exempted from federal rules and widened small-business regulatory analyses. The benefit is real, but it comes by weakening rules that also protect small businesses' employees, customers, and competitors.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and energy-intensive industry subject to EPA rules
industries.note: The bill excluded greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act's definition of air pollutant and streamlined refinery permitting, removing compliance costs by eliminating climate rules.
The bill would freeze new significant rules until unemployment fell, require congressional approval of major rules, sunset unreviewed rules every eight years, and expand litigation against agencies.
